questions.prompt: You cut your window in half by deleting sections from `CLAUDE.md`. A week later Claude stops following a check you deleted, and you never notice. What actually went wrong?
options: The window got too small for Claude to reason about
You deleted instead of relocating, and had no capability test to catch it
Deleting from `CLAUDE.md` always invalidates the cache and confuses the model
Claude forgot the rule because it was compacted away
questions.explanation: Reduction is relocation: the fact needs a home that loads it back, and a test that fails if it is gone. Deleting passes the size test and fails the capability test silently. Option A inverts the lesson — the window was too *full*, not too small. Option C confuses caching with capability; the cache is not why the rule stopped being followed. Option D blames compaction, but the rule was deleted, not summarized.

questions.prompt: You move a research task that reads twelve files into a subagent. What is the honest way to prove capability survived?
options: Confirm the subagent definition file exists
Run a real task that needs the research and confirm it completes, with only the summary in your window
Check that the twelve files are still in the repository
Measure that the main window shrank
questions.explanation: The proof is a task that would fail if the capability were lost, run for real, with the reads happening in the subagent's window and only the summary returning. Option A proves a file exists, not that the capability works. Option C proves the files exist, not that they are read. Option D is the *reduction* measurement, not the *capability* proof — the two are separate claims.

questions.prompt: A convention applies only to files under `packages/api/` and is used on maybe one task in ten. Which home gives the lowest standing cost without losing it?
options: A skill invoked on every task
questions.explanation: A path-scoped rule loads only when a matching file is read, so nine tasks in ten never pay for it while the tenth gets it automatically. Option A pays every session. Option C would load it on every task if invoked, and requires the user to remember to invoke it. Option D is a startup block; the convention is directory-specific, so auto memory is the wrong trigger.

questions.prompt: After a large reshuffle of your context, the next turn is slow and expensive even though the window is now smaller. What is the most likely cause?
options: A smaller context always runs slower on the first turn
The reshuffle changed the request's prefix, so the cache had to rebuild
The removed content corrupted the session
Claude is re-reading the deleted files
questions.explanation: Changing what sits in the prefix changes the exact start of the request, so everything after it is reprocessed — a one-time rebuild. This is why Lesson 89 comes before this one. Option A has no mechanism. Option C invents corruption. Option D is impossible to observe as a cost here and is not what the prefix rule describes.
